How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same — Keep the participants and their event roles distinct from the subject and the first words of the sentence

In 'The bicycle was repaired by Maya', who does the repairing?
column2:
How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same — Keep the participants and their event roles distinct from the subject and the first words of the sentence

In our example, Maya does the repairing and the bicycle is affected. Those are roles in the event. In the active sentence, Maya is also the grammatical subject.

Switch to passive. The bicycle becomes the subject. Maya is still the doer.

Maya

Maya remains the doer. The bicycle is the passive subject and the affected thing.

Grammatical subject and doer are different roles.

How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same — Change the sentence, not the event

These past-simple passives use was + past participle: was repaired, or was painted. A by-phrase can name the doer.

The gate was painted by the team.

'Was painted' is passive. Merely reversing the names changes who did what.

Affected thing + was + past participle, with an optional by-phrase.

column2:
How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same — Omitting the doer loses some information

'The bicycle was repaired' leaves the doer unstated. It can suit a story about the bicycle when who repaired it is unknown, obvious or unimportant.

That shorter sentence does not tell its reader that Maya did it.

No

Unstated is not the same as nonexistent.

How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same — Choose the form that connects the story

How can two sentences describe the same event but start differently?
column2:
How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same — Choose the form that connects the story

If the gate is already your topic, 'The gate was painted' keeps that thread. If you are describing the team's work, the active sentence may fit better.

Passive is a choice about presentation. It is not automatically better, vaguer or more formal in every context.

The grammatical subject can change while event roles stay the same. A passive makes the affected thing the subject; an optional by-phrase names the doer.
  • Separate subject from doer
  • Keep the event roles intact
  • Notice what an omitted doer leaves unstated

Use context, not a blanket ban on passive voice.
